payload.problem_addressed: How to learn the procedural control (which admissible tableau edit to try, keep, or undo) that drives clausal connection-tableau theorem proving, rather than relying on a fixed hand-built search strategy (e.g. leanCoP's depth-first, program-order backtracking).
payload.method_summary: The paper casts connection-tableau construction as a deterministic transition system whose actions are exactly the sound calculus rule applications (start/extension/reduction/factorization) and their undos; a policy chooses among the enabled actions at each state. Found proofs (from any behavior policy, e.g. leanCoP) are replayed from the empty tableau to relabel just the successful path as an expert demonstration, discarding all failed search. A graph neural network (relational GCN over a typed proof-state graph with hash-consed syntax nodes) scores each valid candidate edit from [edit-type embedding; source node embedding; target node embedding], softmaxed into a policy distribution and trained by cross-entropy 'proof cloning' (behavioral cloning). This is iterated DAgger-style ('proof aggregation'): each round runs the current policy, collects newly found proofs, replays them, and retrains from scratch. Three policy variants (markov/dfs/id) differ only in how much search scaffolding (memory) restricts the action space at inference time.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces a general framing in which a proof calculus induces a transition system and a proof procedure becomes a stateful policy over it, making the soundness of any policy automatic and letting standard policy-learning methods (imitation learning, DAgger) apply directly to theorem proving. It proposes 'proof cloning' plus 'proof aggregation': extracting supervised (state, action) demonstrations purely by replaying found proofs (never failed search), and iteratively retraining a graph-neural-network edit-scorer on self-found proofs. It studies three policies that differ only in how much search scaffolding (memory) restricts their action space, isolating the effect of learning from the effect of imposed search structure. Empirically it shows a single trained scorer, evaluated zero-shot across problems, consistently beats the leanCoP baseline across corpora and option profiles.
key_architecture_choices: Relational graph convolution (R-GCN style) over a typed proof-state graph with syntax nodes (term/atom/variable/symbol) and occurrence nodes (clause/literal/goal), with per-relation transforms and reverse edges for bidirectional flow
Hash-consing of syntax nodes so identical ground structure shares one node, and node features encode only type/arity (never symbol identity), making the encoding invariant to signature renaming
Matrix (problem) subgraph is encoded once and cached; only tableau goal nodes are re-encoded as the tableau grows, keeping incremental updates cheap

Candidate edits scored by a shared MLP head over [edit-type embedding; source node embedding; target node embedding], where source/target are literal graph endpoints already present in the encoded graph (a pointer-like scoring over structural roles rather than a free-form output)
Explicit separation of transition-system state (the tableau) from policy memory (stack/depth-bound/etc.), yielding three policy variants (markov, dfs, id) with increasingly restricted action spaces
DAgger-style iterative retraining ('proof aggregation'): each round retrains from scratch on all trajectories replayed from proofs found so far
datasets: M2k (Kaliszyk-Urban Mizar line)
MPTP2078-bushy (MPTP)
TPTP v9.2.1 (FOF problems)
metrics: Solved-problem coverage (count of problems reaching a closed tableau within budget)
Steps (average number of transition steps over successful runs)
New / Lost problems relative to the leanCoP baseline
Training accuracy
payload.headline_results: Within a fixed 1,000-step / 120-second budget, learned policies solve up to 46% more problems than leanCoP and reach proofs in an order of magnitude fewer steps; a learned policy beats the leanCoP baseline in every corpus/option-profile row tested (M2k, MPTP, TPTP), and training the scorer to convergence (vs. early stopping) recovers most of the retention (proofs lost relative to baseline) that early-stopped training gives up.
claimed_advantages: Soundness is guaranteed structurally: any policy that only acts through the transition function T produces valid partial tableaux, so a closed terminal state is automatically a checkable proof

Demonstrations are recovered automatically and are effectively optimal: replay keeps only the proof-producing actions of a successful run, discarding the demonstrator's failed search, so imitation trains on a refined/optimal sub-policy rather than the noisy behavior policy
Symbol-independent, signature-invariant encoding lets one trained scorer generalize zero-shot across problems not seen in training
Consistent gains across every tested corpus and option profile isolate that the improvement comes from learning, not from a particular search configuration
limitations: Training labels come only from the successful path of found proofs, so undo/backtrack actions are never demonstrated; policies (especially the least-restricted πmarkov) are never trained to decide when to undo, which drives most of their lost-proof (retention) penalty
The imitation 'expert' is weaker than a queryable DAgger oracle: unsolved problems yield no labels at all, and tableau states outside any found proof's path remain permanently unlabeled
No held-out validation set is used; the protocol optimizes for fitting demonstrations exactly and measures generalization only as zero-shot transfer coverage

The evaluation deliberately holds calculus/implementation fixed and does not compare against other connection provers or saturation systems, so it is not (and does not claim to be) a competition-level result
Coverage gains plateau after a few proof-aggregation iterations, since remaining unsolved problems fall outside the patterns of already-found proofs or beyond the step budget
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The core mechanism is directly transferable to hexgen's structural-validity problem: the transition-system framing enumerates, at every decoding step, only the actions the calculus admits (analogous to masking the DSL decoder to only compile-admissible block/sweep/projection commands), giving validity 'for free' by construction rather than by post-hoc checking. 'Proof cloning' from replayed successful trajectories (discard all failed search, keep only the winning path) mirrors hexgen's supervised imitation on inverse-factory-synthesized programs, and 'proof aggregation' is a concrete DAgger-style repair/self-improvement loop (retrain on trajectories from proofs the current policy itself finds) that could drive a rejection-sampled SFT flywheel against hexgen's frozen verifier, matching problems 1 and 6 in our problem statement. The edit-scoring head — an MLP over [edit-type embedding; source-node embedding; target-node embedding] where source/target are graph nodes already produced by a GNN encoder — is architecturally close to hexgen's pointer/copy heads addressing faces of the input B-rep graph, and the hash-consing / type-only node features used for signature-invariance is a related (though not identical) idea to rotation/pose-invariant encoding. Finally, the paper's diagnosis that omitting backtrack labels from proof replay starves the policy of undo/repair supervision is a concrete cautionary lesson for any repair/edit-distillation scheme hexgen builds from best-of-N verifier-passing rollouts.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is a formal automated-theorem-proving paper (logic, not geometry/CAD) with no B-rep or meshing content whatsoever — everything above is a mechanism-level transfer, not a domain-level one, so weight it as inspiration for the training/decoding loop rather than as a directly reusable component. The most exportable idea is the coupling of (a) a calculus/grammar-restricted valid-action space with (b) imitation purely from replayed successful trajectories with (c) DAgger-style iterative self-improvement against that same admissibility check — this maps well onto hexgen's verifier-gated best-of-N + imitation setup. The explicit finding that action spaces lacking undo/backtrack supervision hurt retention is worth flagging for our own edit-distillation/repair design. Code is released, which would let someone actually inspect the R-GCN scorer and DAgger loop implementation if deeper borrowing is wanted.
dependencies_on_other_methods: Relational graph convolutional networks (Schlichtkrull et al. 2018)
leanCoP baseline prover and its option profiles (Otten 2008; Otten 2010)

payload.problem_addressed: The paper studies whether spending more inference-time compute (wider beam search or more samples with voting) can substitute for a larger model size when an LLM's outputs must satisfy a strict formal grammar, using grammar-constrained text-to-SQL as the test case.
payload.method_summary: Four sizes of Qwen2.5-Instruct (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B; 4-bit NF4 quantized) are evaluated on the full Spider dev set (1034 examples) under schema-aware grammar-constrained decoding, which masks any token that would make the output invalid SQL or reference a nonexistent table/column. At matched inference budgets B in {1,2,4,8}, two ways of spending that budget are compared: beam search (keep the B highest-scoring partial hypotheses, expand and prune each step, with a length penalty of -2.0) versus sample+vote (draw B samples at temperature 0.7/top-p 0.9, execute each against the database, discard failures, and return the query giving the modal execution result). Differences are tested with McNemar's exact test on paired predictions; individual accuracies are reported with 95% Wilson score intervals.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper shows that under grammar-constrained decoding, beam search is never significantly worse than sample+vote (self-consistency) at matched inference budget, and is significantly better in 11 of 16 tested configurations -- the opposite of prior unconstrained-setting findings that favor self-consistency/sampling. It shows the grammar constraint itself can cost accuracy relative to unconstrained greedy decoding when the grammar's coverage is incomplete, causing correct, executable queries to be rejected and forcing worse forced continuations. It also shows additional inference-time compute (wider beams or more samples) reliably improves accuracy, especially for smaller models, but in 2 of the 3 tested model-size gaps this compute increase does not fully substitute for using a larger model.
key_architecture_choices: Context-free-grammar constrained decoding: a schema-aware grammar masks any next token that would make the output invalid SQL or reference nonexistent tables/columns, renormalizing over the admitted set
Beam search retaining B highest-scoring partial hypotheses per step, with a -2.0 length penalty to counter the fact the grammar never forces termination
Sample+vote (execution-based self-consistency): draw B samples at temperature 0.7 / top-p 0.9, execute each against the target database, discard failures, return the modal execution result
4-bit (NF4) quantization applied uniformly across all evaluated model sizes
datasets: Spider text-to-SQL benchmark, full development set (1034 examples)
metrics: Execution accuracy (prediction correct iff its result set matches the gold query's, order-sensitive only when gold has ORDER BY)
McNemar's exact test on paired predictions for statistical significance between configurations
95% Wilson score confidence intervals on individual accuracy estimates
payload.headline_results: At matched budget, beam search is significantly more accurate than sample+vote in 11 of 16 model-size x budget cells and never significantly less accurate. Wider beams give only modest gains that shrink with model size (~0.15 absolute accuracy for 1.5B down to ~0.05 for 7B at width 8). At a budget of 8, extra inference compute closes only 50-76% of the accuracy gap to the next larger model size, and only 1 of 3 size-ladder steps (1.5B->3B) is fully bridged by compute alone. Grammar incompleteness costs accuracy: at 3B and 7B the unconstrained greedy baseline beats budget-1 grammar-constrained decoding (0.477 vs 0.445; 0.643 vs 0.600), traced to the grammar rejecting valid, correct SQL it cannot derive (e.g. certain IN lists, IS NOT NULL, outer joins, informal aliases).
claimed_advantages: Sample+vote is never significantly more accurate than beam search at matched budget, and beam search is significantly ahead in the majority of tested configurations
A negative length penalty alone is sufficient to control non-termination in grammar-constrained beam search even in a grammar that never forces an end-of-sequence token
Inference-time compute gives the largest accuracy boosts for the smallest models (up to ~2.2x at B=8 for 0.5B/1.5B), so compute scaling is most valuable exactly where model capacity is weakest
limitations: Experiments were limited to one model family (Qwen2.5-Instruct), one benchmark (Spider), and a single decoding run per configuration
Sample+vote uses a single random seed per configuration, so intrinsic run-to-run variability of sampling is not characterized (left to future work)
Only one temperature (0.7) for sample+vote was tested; a full temperature sweep was not performed

The specific grammar used is acknowledged to be incomplete (cannot express certain IN-list forms, IS NOT NULL, outer joins, informal aliases), which the authors show directly costs accuracy -- a property of their grammar implementation rather than of grammar-constrained decoding in general

Exploratory (unreported) experiments suggested results on smaller data subsets favored sample+vote over beam search, an effect that vanished only at the full n=1034, implying small-benchmark evaluations of this comparison could mislead
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Directly relevant to hexgen's core structural-validity problem (grammar/schema-constrained autoregressive DSL generation, verifier-screened best-of-N): (1) the paper's central finding -- that under a hard grammar constraint, beam search matches or beats sampling+execution-voting at every matched compute budget -- suggests hexgen's best-of-N-plus-verifier pipeline may benefit from adding or substituting a beam-search-style search over partial block/sweep/projection programs (possibly verifier- or partial-score-guided) rather than relying purely on independent sampling, since it targets the same structured/schema-constrained generation setting (problem 7) and constrained-decoding search-strategy tradeoff (problem 1). (2) Its diagnosis that an incomplete constraint grammar silently rejects valid, correct outputs and forces globally worse continuations is a concrete, transferable risk to audit in hexgen's DSL grammar/pointer-copy constraint set -- incompleteness there could be costing structural validity the same way, independent of model capacity. (3) The execution-based vote mechanism (group candidates by execution outcome, take the mode) is structurally analogous to hexgen's frozen verifier and worth comparing against beam-search-plus-verifier selection at matched compute. (4) The finding that inference compute only partially substitutes for model parameters is a relevant data point for hexgen's own tradeoff between the 27M-parameter model's capacity and the cost of larger best-of-N verifier passes.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is a small, focused empirical study (two authors, one benchmark, one model family) rather than a new method paper -- treat its numeric findings as suggestive rather than general, per the authors' own stated limitations. The text-to-SQL setting differs substantially from hexgen's pointer/copy-over-B-rep-graph decoding (different vocabulary structure, different grammar complexity, different notion of 'execution'), so the specific magnitudes will not transfer, but the qualitative mechanisms (beam search advantage under hard constraints; grammar-incompleteness cost; partial-only compute-for-parameters substitution) are architecture-agnostic claims worth testing directly against hexgen's own verifier and DSL grammar. No code repository is mentioned/linked in the text, so replication would require reimplementing the beam-search/sample+vote comparison harness. Worth flagging to whoever owns hexgen's DSL grammar: run a coverage audit analogous to this paper's re-parsing analysis to check whether the hex-meshing DSL constraint set can express every valid block/sweep/projection program the deterministic mesher would accept.
dependencies_on_other_methods: Grammar-constrained decoding via context-free-grammar token masking (Geng et al. 2023; Willard and Louf 2023)
Self-consistency / sample+vote sampling method (Wang et al. 2023)

provenance.problem_addressed: we examine the constrained case of this “model size vs. inference compute” trade-off, in which the model outputs are constrained by a strict grammar at inference time
provenance.method_summary: We experiment with two approaches to varying inference compute: (i) beam search with a variable number of beams; and (ii) sample+vote
provenance.key_architecture_choices: Beam search maintains B partial hypotheses, expands each at every step, and retains the B highest-scoring continuations.
provenance.datasets: the full development set of 1,034 examples from the Spider benchmark [Yu et al., 2018]
provenance.metrics: A prediction is correct when it and the gold query return the same result set on D... Execution accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions.
provenance.headline_results: beam search is significantly more accurate than sample+vote in eleven and significantly less accurate in none
provenance.claimed_advantages: Sample+vote is never significantly more accurate than beam search.
provenance.limitations: Our experiments were limited in scope to one model family (Qwen2.5-Instruct), one benchmark (Spider), and a single decoding run per configuration.
provenance.implementation_cost_estimate: Two ways of spending a computational budget B on this grammar-constrained model are compared.
provenance.dependencies_on_other_methods: Our evaluation employs the Qwen2.5-Instruct family of models [Qwen Team, 2024], with sizes s at 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, and 7B parameters.

payload.problem_addressed: LLMs prompted to write programs in a target-fixed, training-data-rare grammar (a DSL) usually emit programs that break the grammar or fail the given input-output spec, and existing LLM-guided enumerative synthesizers compile LLM proposals into a static, context-free rule-frequency prior that ignores where a construct belongs and prunes any rule the (possibly wrong) proposals never used.
payload.method_summary: Narcissus samples a handful of LLM program proposals once per task, parses them into ASTs and repairs grammar-violating sub-terms into typed holes, mines recurring subtrees into grammar-extending macro-rules, then compiles the repaired trees into a context-aware heuristic H(r|p,Pi) that scores each candidate-program expansion using three combined signals -- prefix alignment (do proposals sharing the same root-to-hole context use rule r), sub-program reuse (does r rebuild a fragment the proposals repeat), and regularization (a Gaussian mixture over proposal program sizes plus a positive floor C that keeps every grammar rule reachable) -- and this heuristic then guides either a genetic top-down search or a cost-guided bottom-up beam search, with no further LLM calls during search.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper contributes a context-aware heuristic that scores each grammar-rule expansion by prefix alignment, sub-program reuse, and regularization instead of a single global rule frequency, cheap enough to consult at millions of search expansions. It contributes a pipeline that turns raw, often ungrammatical LLM proposal text into grammar-aware guidance by repairing proposals against the grammar and mining their recurring fragments into grammar extensions. It also contributes evidence across five program-synthesis domains and two search backends that this context-aware approximation beats static LLM-guided synthesis and direct re-prompting, and that the regularization term makes the method safe (no worse than unguided search) even when proposals are poor.
key_architecture_choices: Keeps LLM proposals as parsed, grammar-repaired abstract syntax trees rather than collapsing them into rule-frequency counts
Repairs ungrammatical proposal sub-terms into typed holes top-down rather than discarding the whole proposal
Mines subtrees recurring >=2 times across proposals into macro-rules that extend the grammar (G+)
Heuristic combines three fixed-weight signals: prefix alignment (context match), sub-program reuse (context-free fragment reuse), and regularization (program-size Gaussian mixture + positive floor)
A strictly positive floor C in the regularization term guarantees every grammar rule keeps nonzero score, so no rule is ever pruned from search
Two interchangeable search backends: a genetic (mutation-based, top-down) search and a cost-guided bottom-up beam search extending HySynth's architecture
For harder domains (BV, ARC, ARGA) the heuristic is dropped unchanged into an existing divide-and-conquer synthesizer (EUSolver)
datasets: SLIA (SyGuS string-manipulation track)
BV (SyGuS bit-vector track, PBE_BV_Track_2018)
DeepCoder (DC, list-manipulation domain)
ARC (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, over the Hodel DSL)
ARGA (object-centric ARC subset)
GPT-4o proposal set released by HySynth for SLIA/ARGA subsets
Proposals sampled from DeepSeek-V4-Flash, its reasoning variant, and Haiku-4.5
metrics: Tasks solved (final count within budget)
Programs enumerated vs. tasks-solved curve
Wall-clock time vs. tasks-solved curve
Normalized area under the solve curve (AUC) in log10(budget) space, as % of benchmark solved
Raw proposal accuracy (fraction of tasks solved by at least one sampled proposal, i.e. proposal support)
payload.headline_results: Across five domains and two search backends Narcissus beats the static rule-frequency prior at every enumeration/time budget and every level of proposal support, reaching proposal-like programs about an order of magnitude sooner (about 12x sooner in programs enumerated on SLIA); on full ARC it solves 40% of tasks vs. 13% for the raw grammar-valid proposals and 12 for the static heuristic; on weak-support BV Narcissus solves 350/587 tasks (above unguided enumeration's 302) while the static priors collapse to 102 and 57; on SLIA (70-task, GPT-4o) Narcissus+Genetic reaches 51.4/70 solved (32.2% AUC) vs. Static+BUS 48.0 (23.5% AUC); re-prompting the LLM to self-correct gains only ~1-3 extra tasks.
claimed_advantages: No LLM call during search -- guidance costs only a tree lookup per expansion, unlike LLM-in-the-loop search methods whose LLM-call count grows with search effort

Regularization floor means no grammar rule is ever pruned, so misleading/weak proposals only delay the solution rather than making the task unsolvable; worst case degrades gracefully to unguided enumeration
Outperforms static (context-free) LLM-approximation baselines (HySynth-style) at every proposal-support level, including when proposals are weak or scarce
A cheap/weak proposal model plus Narcissus search can match or beat a stronger proposal model under a static heuristic (DeepSeek+Narcissus rivals GPT-4o+static on SLIA)
Heuristic drops unchanged into existing synthesizer architectures (genetic mutation, bottom-up beam, EUSolver divide-and-conquer)
limitations: Signal weights and the regularization floor are fixed at 1 for all domains after a sweep on SLIA only; the paper notes a per-task weighting based on proposal properties is left to future work
Mined sub-program fragments are discarded after each task rather than shared/reused across tasks
In bottom-up beam search there is no root-to-hole path when the root is built last, so prefix alignment must be redefined/anchored on the sub-program itself rather than applied natively

Ablations show no single signal dominates in every regime -- which signal is load-bearing (prefix alignment vs. sub-program reuse) inverts with proposal size/quality, so a single fixed combination is a compromise
Evaluated only on symbolic program-synthesis DSLs (strings, bit-vectors, list ops, ARC grid DSL) with CFG-based grammars and hole-filling search, not on neural sequence/graph decoders
Requires an explicit context-free grammar and a repair procedure that can parse and complete arbitrary proposal text against it
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The core mechanism -- treating a set of imperfect candidate programs (here LLM 'proposals', analogous to hexgen's best-of-N decoder rollouts) as structural evidence rather than answers, repairing them into valid partial ASTs with typed holes, and using a cheap, context-conditioned score (does this same local context recur across candidates? does this fragment recur across candidates? stay close to candidates' size distribution, with a floor so no option is ever fully excluded) to guide a downstream search -- is directly relevant to our structural-validity problem (#1). Concretely: (a) the 'regularization floor that keeps every rule reachable' is a transferable design lesson for any verifier-guided search/repair over hexgen programs, avoiding a search that gets stuck when best-of-N samples never used a needed block/sweep/projection command; (b) mining recurring sub-programs from multiple sampled rollouts into reusable macro-rules could shortcut generation of common block/sweep motifs; (c) the prefix-alignment idea (score a continuation by whether other same-context candidates continue the same way) is a lightweight, training-free alternative/complement to value/critic-guided search or MCTS over program prefixes for repairing a hexgen model's own broken rollouts, since it requires no LLM/critic calls, only tree lookups over already-sampled candidates plus the frozen verifier for final acceptance.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is a symbolic program-synthesis paper (SyGuS/ARC-style CFG-grammar domains), not CAD/mesh or neural-graph-decoding work, so nothing here is a drop-in component for hexgen -- the transfer is at the level of a general 'search around sampled proposals with a cheap, never-fully-pruning heuristic' pattern rather than a specific architecture. It assumes a hole-filling AST/CFG formalism; mapping 'context' (root-to-hole rule path) onto hexgen's autoregressive pointer/copy decoding over a face graph would need real adaptation work, since hexgen's grammar is not a classic CFG and its 'holes' are pointer choices over graph nodes plus a coordinate vocabulary rather than typed nonterminals. Also note the method is purely symbolic/counting-based (no learned model, no fine-tuning), so it does not touch domain-gap, rotation-robustness, or copy-mechanism concerns; its closest relevance is the structural-validity / execution-guided search bucket. Code and cached proposals are public, which lowers the cost of prototyping a similar heuristic offline against hexgen's own verifier output.

payload.problem_addressed: Generative modeling of 2D residential roof structure, represented as vertex-edge graphs in top-down view, across three regimes: unconditional roof graph generation, footprint-conditioned generation, and image-guided reconstruction from aerial imagery.
payload.method_summary: RoofDiT is a two-stage pipeline built on the GSDiff framework: a conditional diffusion transformer denoises noisy node states into roof-graph vertices (optionally conditioned on footprint vertices and/or pretrained DINOv2 aerial-image features), and a separate, unchanged edge-prediction module then infers pairwise connectivity over the generated node set to produce the final graph. Node generation is augmented with relative geometry-aware attention (an MLP maps pairwise coordinate offsets/distance/direction between nodes into per-head attention-logit biases), multimodal conditioning (footprint vertices concatenated into the node token sequence for self-attention; image features injected via cross-attention), and a roof alignment regularizer that penalizes each node's distance to the nearest of four canonical line families (horizontal, vertical, two diagonals), added as an auxiliary diffusion-training loss.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper formulates roof structure modeling as a generative problem over 2D roof graphs and proposes a diffusion-transformer prior that supports unconditional generation, footprint-conditioned generation, and image-guided reconstruction within a single model by varying the conditioning signal. It introduces relative geometry-aware attention, multimodal (footprint + image) conditioning, and a roof alignment regularizer tailored to recurring horizontal/vertical/diagonal roof patterns. The authors benchmark against a diffusion baseline (GSDiff), a geometric baseline (straight skeleton), and image-based reconstruction baselines (HEAT, RoofMapNet), showing improved distributional realism over GSDiff, a validity/flexibility tradeoff against straight skeleton, and competitive but not state-of-the-art reconstruction versus HEAT.
key_architecture_choices: Two-stage decoupled generation: diffusion transformer for node/vertex generation followed by a separate, off-the-shelf edge-prediction module (kept unchanged from GSDiff) for connectivity
Relative geometry-aware attention: pairwise node features (coordinate offsets, Euclidean distance, normalized direction) passed through a small MLP to produce per-head additive attention-logit biases

Multimodal conditioning via token concatenation (footprint vertices joined into the node token stream for self-attention) plus cross-attention injection of frozen pretrained DINOv2 ViT-S/14 image features with positional encoding

Roof alignment regularizer: auxiliary loss penalizing each node's distance to its nearest support line among four canonical families (x=const, y=const, x+y=const, x-y=const), with time-dependent weighting across diffusion steps, added to the diffusion loss
Preprocessing canonicalization: rotating each roof so the longest footprint edge aligns to a fixed reference axis, then snapping near-axis-aligned edges
datasets: Residential roof dataset from Ren et al. [17]: 1,926 train / 249 validation / 223 test samples, with paired aerial imagery and derived 2D roof graphs (vertices = roof junctions, edges = roofline segments)
metrics: Roof Valid Rate
Planar Rate

#Components, Crossings, Dangling nodes
payload.headline_results: Unconditional: RoofDiT beats GSDiff on all reported metrics, notably FID 53.954→45.329 and KID 31.210→23.442. Footprint-conditioned: vs. straight skeleton, RoofDiT lowers Node Count MAE (2.008→1.002) and Face Count Error (1.430→0.444) and raises Edge F1 (0.960→0.981); under best-of-5 sampling, face F1 rises 0.798→0.886 and valid rate 0.841→0.930, though straight skeleton remains stronger on node F1@5, matched IoU, planar rate, and single-draw valid rate. Image-guided: HEAT is the overall strongest baseline; adding footprint conditioning to RoofDiT substantially improves it over aerial-only input (node F1 42.6→70.3, edge F1 78.4→98.4, face F1 63.5→82.4, node count MAE 2.23→0.90).
claimed_advantages: A single model supports unconditional, footprint-conditioned, and image-guided generation by varying the conditioning signal

Learned generative prior captures a broader, more realistic diversity of plausible roof organizations than a deterministic geometric construction (straight skeleton) or a simpler diffusion baseline (GSDiff)
Best-of-K sampling exploits the fact that a footprint does not uniquely determine roof topology, recovering good solutions even when the top-1 draw does not
Relative geometry-aware attention and the roof alignment regularizer are claimed to improve geometric fidelity by injecting explicit pairwise/structural geometric priors into the transformer
limitations: Validity is encouraged through learning rather than guaranteed by construction, so RoofDiT is weaker than the deterministic straight-skeleton baseline on strict validity, planarity, and matched IoU under footprint conditioning
Operates only on planar 2D roof graphs; does not directly recover 3D geometry, roof heights, or watertight building models
In image-guided reconstruction, HEAT still outperforms RoofDiT overall on precise agreement with ground truth
Single-sample (non best-of-K) generation does not always select the closest solution, indicating a consistency/sample-selection weakness rather than a capacity limitation
Image-guided comparison across methods is noted as not strictly controlled, since baselines use pixel-aligned annotations while RoofDiT uses canonicalized graph representations
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The relative geometry-aware attention mechanism (a small MLP mapping pairwise node offset/distance/direction into per-head attention-logit biases) is directly transferable to our graph-transformer B-rep encoder and pointer/copy heads: it is a lightweight, general way to inject explicit geometric relations (e.g., face-centroid offsets, adjacency angles) into attention over the face graph, which is squarely in our category-4 interest (Graphormer-style edge-biased attention / addressing into an input set) and could help disambiguate congruent/symmetric faces when pointing. The roof alignment regularizer — an auxiliary differentiable loss that softly penalizes deviation from a small set of canonical geometric relations during training — is a transferable pattern for shaping generation toward our own hard verifier criteria (e.g., scaled-Jacobian/aspect-ratio bounds, feature-edge capture) as a soft training signal that could reduce the reject rate before best-of-N verifier screening, rather than relying on rejection alone. The paper's explicit framing that 'validity is encouraged through learning rather than guaranteed by construction' and its reliance on a downstream deterministic/verifiable stage (edge prediction, or in our case a frozen verifier) to make up the gap reinforces our architectural bet on pairing a learned generator with a frozen, machine-checkable verifier rather than expecting the generator alone to guarantee validity. The multimodal token-concatenation conditioning strategy (treating footprint vertices as additional tokens in the same representation space as generated nodes) is a loosely analogous idea to conditioning our decoder jointly on multiple structured input sources.
payload.reviewer_notes: This paper is out of our core domain (2D roof vector graphs from aerial imagery/footprints, computer vision/GIS application, not mechanical B-rep or hex-meshing), so most of its dataset, metrics, and baselines (GSDiff, straight skeleton, HEAT, RoofMapNet) are not directly reusable. The value here is narrowly mechanistic: the relative geometry-aware attention module and the soft alignment regularizer are small, self-contained architectural ideas worth mining rather than a paper to adopt wholesale. Note the dataset scale (~2,400 total roofs) is a similar order of magnitude to typical CAD auto-labeled corpora, so the paper's implicit lesson that a learned prior plus best-of-K sampling can partially compensate for limited deterministic guarantees is relevant context, though not a novel mechanism per se. No code repository is mentioned in the provided text (checked references and body), so mechanism reuse would require reimplementation from the equations given (Eqs. 2-5), which are fully specified and simple enough to reimplement quickly.
dependencies_on_other_methods: Builds on the two-stage node-generation-then-edge-prediction framework of GSDiff [9], reusing its edge prediction stage unchanged
Uses a frozen pretrained DINOv2 ViT-S/14 image encoder [15] for aerial-image conditioning

payload.problem_addressed: The paper addresses executable video-editing planning: turning a brief, a real clip pool with captions/metadata, optional music metadata, and an explicit constraint ledger into an executable edit plan (a sequence of structured JSON-Patch edits over a typed timeline), as opposed to prior workflow systems that just wrap a prompted frozen frontier LLM and never train the planning policy itself.
payload.method_summary: RefineCut is a two-stage training recipe plus a closed-loop inference procedure for a compact open-weight LoRA-tuned planner (Qwen3-8B-Instruct, also tested on Llama-3.1-8B/GLM-4-9B). Stage 1 (verifier-replayed teacher bootstrap) canonicalizes noisy multi-branch trajectories from three frontier API teachers, replays every candidate branch through a deterministic verifier that applies the patch and recomputes an explicit constraint ledger, and keeps only verifier-best branches as SFT targets plus step- and trajectory-level DPO preference pairs (Mixed-Pref). Stage 2 (RefineCut-Evo) has the student itself sample K=4 candidate repairs per training state, scores each with the same verifier plus a fixed task rubric (ER1-ER7), and trains with DPO on high-margin (verifier+rubric) chosen/rejected pairs. At inference the planner and verifier run a closed Apply/Verify loop for at most T=3 repair steps with no teacher calls.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper formulates executable video-editing planning and releases RefineCut-Bench, a benchmark with real clip/music metadata, explicit constraint ledgers, and multi-teacher trajectories. It proposes verifier-replayed trajectory distillation, which canonicalizes and replays noisy frontier-teacher branches through a deterministic verifier to produce verified SFT targets and preference pairs instead of imitating a teacher's unreliable first-choice branch. It introduces RefineCut-Evo, a verifier-centered, rubric-structured self-improvement stage trained with DPO on the student's own scored repair candidates. The authors show the resulting 8B open-weight planner substantially outperforms raw imitation, transfers across three backbones, and matches or exceeds its frontier API teachers when run in an identical closed verifier loop.
key_architecture_choices: Backbone: Qwen3-8B-Instruct (also Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, GLM-4-9B) fine-tuned with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning

A deterministic, frozen verifier applies each patch and recomputes an explicit constraint ledger (item_id, type, spec, satisfied, evidence) rather than using a learned LLM judge as the primary training signal

Two-stage training: SFT on verifier-best replayed branches, then DPO on verifier/rubric-scored preference pairs (mixed step-level and trajectory-level pairs in Stage 1; high-margin self-generated pairs in Stage 2)
Branch/candidate scoring is a fixed weighted sum of six deterministic signals (delta constraint-satisfaction, targeted repair, required-clip recall, patch-apply success, no-regression, locality)
Closed-loop deployment: planner and verifier iterate Apply/Verify for at most T=3 steps at inference with zero teacher/API calls
datasets: RefineCut-Bench (3,578 canonical tasks, 7,971 captioned clips, 499 music tracks, explicit constraint ledgers) built by the authors
Common-100 (main evaluation subset) and dev100 (checkpoint selection)
Canonical-clean subset (N=92) held out to rule out canonical-id train/test overlap
Human50 (50 free-form human-written briefs with LLM-drafted, human-revised ledgers) for out-of-distribution instruction-style validation
metrics: Video-Editing Score (VES): fixed weighted sum of FinalCSR, HardPass, PASR, ReqClipRecall, DurationPass@2s, TimelineValidity, NoRegression
schema validity, patch applicability, timeline validity, constraint satisfaction, hard-constraint pass, clip grounding, duration/pacing, no-regression, and convergence
Converged@3 (terminal constraint satisfaction >= 0.8 within 3 repair steps)
Blind rendered-preview human A/B preference score and inter-annotator kappa
Blind API-judge win rate as an external agreement check
payload.headline_results: verifier-replayed distillation lifts the planner from 0.6200.620 to 0.8580.858 on the protocol-specific Video-Editing Score and RefineCut-Evo reaches 0.9240.924
claimed_advantages: The gain comes from replay filtering out branches that fail on execution, not from more data.
Verifier-scored self-improvement (RefineCut-Evo) fixes all-or-nothing whole-plan properties (HardPass, duration, convergence) that single-patch SFT/DPO on teacher traces does not.
Verified SFT recovers performance on all three backbones tested while raw imitation is flat or harmful, showing the mechanism is not backbone-specific.
The final 8B closed-loop planner matches or exceeds two of its three frontier API teachers and ties the third, at a fraction of the per-task latency and with no inference-time API calls.
limitations: it cannot judge whether a cut is tasteful or a story lands, which only the rendered-preview study touches
VES is an in-protocol measure rather than an independent absolute quality score, since the same verifier supplies training-time replay, closed-loop feedback, and evaluation

Evidence covers only the compact 8B-9B model regime, three model families, three task families, and one asset pool; the preference-training stages are only run on Qwen3-8B
RefineCut-Evo is offline DPO rather than a full online-RL or EvoLM reproduction
Benchmark briefs and ledgers are LLM-generated under controlled templates (Human50 only partially validates transfer to fully free-form human specifications)
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Strong structural analogy to hexgen's problem #1 (structural validity of generated programs) and #6 (verifier-in-the-loop self-improvement). The core transferable mechanism is 'verifier replay': instead of trusting the sampler's/teacher's first-choice output as a label, replay every candidate through the frozen, machine-checkable verifier and keep only verifier-best candidates as SFT targets -- directly applicable to screening hexgen's inverse-factory-sampled programs and best-of-N candidates before imitation training. Second, the two-stage recipe (SFT on verifier-best examples, then a self-improvement DPO stage where the student itself samples K candidates, gets them verifier+rubric scored, and trains on high-margin chosen/rejected pairs) is a ready template for a post-imitation self-improvement stage for hexgen, using its existing frozen verifier (compiles, zero inverted elements, quality bounds, feature capture, element-budget) as the scoring signal in place of RefineCut's constraint ledger. Third, the paper's decomposed branch-score (delta constraint-satisfaction, targeted repair, required-element recall, applicability, no-regression, locality) is a usable template for turning hexgen's pass/fail verifier checks into a graded scalar reward for ranking/repair. Fourth, their ablation showing verifier-only DPO scoring captures most of the gain (0.909 of 0.924 VES) with a learned/heuristic rubric adding only a small increment is encouraging evidence that a frozen-verifier-only self-improvement loop (no learned rubric) -- matching hexgen's current design -- can still deliver most of the benefit. Weaker, tangential borrow: the DAgger-adjacent framing of 'replay noisy demonstrations through an executor before imitating them' generalizes to hexgen's auto-labeled real-CAD programs from construction templates, which could analogously be verifier-replayed rather than trusted outright.
payload.reviewer_notes: Domain (video-editing planning) is unrelated to CAD/meshing, so nothing here transfers as a ready-made component -- the value is entirely in the training-recipe structure, which closely mirrors hexgen's own plan (imitation from a synthetic/auto-labeled sampler, screened best-of-N against a frozen verifier). The clean separation of 'verifier-only DPO' (0.909) vs. full rubric-margin DPO (0.924) is the most actionable data point: it suggests hexgen's planned frozen-verifier-only setup could capture most of a similar self-improvement gain without needing to build a learned quality rubric. Caveat: their verifier yields rich graded partial-credit (per-entry ledger pass rate), letting branch scoring be a smooth weighted sum; hexgen's verifier checks (compiles, zero inverted elements, Jacobian/aspect bounds, boundary fidelity, feature capture) may need to be combined into an analogous graded scalar (e.g., fraction of checks passed, or a small weighted sum) to replicate this branch-scoring mechanism rather than relying on a single binary pass/fail. Code and benchmark are both publicly released, so the verifier-replay + DPO implementation could be inspected directly as a reference. Reported compute cost is modest (~14.5-23.5 GPU-hours on a single A100 for the core pipeline), suggesting a similar self-improvement stage would be cheap to prototype for hexgen. Also note the paper explicitly flags that verifier-based metrics are in-protocol (not independent), a caution equally applicable to over-trusting a frozen verifier as the sole hexgen training signal without periodic human/held-out audits.

payload.problem_addressed: Given a single trained network for rasterized floorplan vectorization (walls, openings, rooms), the paper studies whether output geometry should be produced by autoregressive sequence emission or by detecting it on dense heatmaps, and separately whether the room-centric vs. wall-first output representation is what determines topological validity/quality.
payload.method_summary: A wall-first network reuses the Raster2Seq backbone (ResNet features + deformable-attention encoder) feeding a grammar/type-masked causal autoregressive decoder that emits walls, rooms (as cycles of wall IDs), and openings, plus a dense branch of three jointly-trained heatmaps (junctions, centerlines, openings) sharing the same encoder. Two readouts are compared on this one trained network: 'emit' (sequence decode + endpoint snapping to junction peaks) and 'detect' (a training-free graph readout that takes junction-heatmap peaks as nodes and centerline-coverage of chords as edges, with domain-calibrated thresholds and optional chaining). A separate room-centric system (Raster2Seq + a deterministic reconciliation step: welding, shared-edge dedup, T-splitting, re-projection) is compared against the wall-first system under matched data/recipe. The paper also introduces a deterministic output-level fusion of the two systems' walls (gated by an ink-purity check) and tests input-side conditioning (feeding one system's draft output as an extra input channel/prefix to the other) under a pre-registered stop rule.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper compares two ways of extracting vector geometry (walls, openings, rooms) from a single trained floorplan-vectorization network -- emitting the geometry as an autoregressive coordinate sequence versus detecting it from dense heatmaps and assembling a graph -- and shows which one wins depends on scan domain and plan size rather than being universally better. It also tests whether the room-centric versus wall-first output representation is what drives topological quality, and finds instead that a deterministic reconciliation/post-processing step and evaluation convention explain most of the difference, with the representation itself contributing mainly a coverage limitation. Building on this, the authors show that combining the two systems' outputs after generation (fusion) helps substantially, while feeding one system's output as an input prior to the other does not. They release an edit-cost evaluation metric and a new redistributable floorplan-vectorization benchmark (ResPlan-FP) along with corrected annotations for an existing dataset.
key_architecture_choices: Grammar/type-masked autoregressive decoder: a type mask at every decoding step restricts the next token to what the output grammar allows, structurally preventing duplicate wall IDs or rooms referencing unemitted walls

Training-free graph readout: converts dense junction/centerline heatmaps into a wall graph via non-max-suppression node extraction + chord-coverage edge test + optional chaining, with no trained parameters and per-domain calibrated thresholds

Shared encoder with two heads: a sequence decoder and a dense multi-heatmap branch (junction/centerline/opening) are trained jointly off one encoder, so both readouts come 'for free' from one trained model
Deterministic reconciliation post-processing (welding, shared-edge dedup, T-splitting, re-projection) that derives a watertight wall set from room-polygon output and eliminates double walls
Deterministic output-level fusion of two systems' outputs, gated by an ink-purity check, with a derived closed-form condition (donor purity > half of base system's F1) for when fusion helps vs. hurts
Edit-cost metric: draft quality scored via a weighted sum of matching-derived edit operations (move ≪ type < create=delete ≪ convert) approximating human correction effort rather than raw F1
datasets: CubiCasa5K (real scans, with released corrected 'skv4' annotations)
Procedurally generated synthetic floorplan set fit to real residential listing statistics (incl. an open-plan tier)
ResPlan / ResPlan-FP (new CC BY 4.0 benchmark of 16,998 plans built from ResPlan, frozen splits)
Structured3D (used only for pretraining initialization)
metrics: Wall/room/opening F1 via Hungarian matching at IoU>=0.5 over a tolerance sweep (0.015-0.08)
Watertightness rate (r_val), read jointly with double-wall count
Edit-cost metric (weighted sum of move/type/create/delete/convert operations)
Paired percentile bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over plans
payload.headline_results: On real scans, the training-free graph/detect readout beats autoregressive sequence decoding on every wall measure (+2.7pp wall F1 at tolerance 0.05, +5.1pp at 0.015), and reading an opening heatmap the decoder never used raises opening F1 from ~0.25 to ~0.64 (2.6x) with no retraining. On clean vector renders the order reverses in favor of sequence decoding by 5-8pp where training covered the render style. A matched-data room-centric system (with reconciliation) and a wall-first system reach comparable wall quality, so representation alone is not the main driver of topological quality. Deterministic output-level fusion of the two systems' outputs raises wall F1 by ~7 points over the best single system, whereas feeding one system's output as an input prior to the other gives no gain.
claimed_advantages: The graph/detect readout requires no additional training (zero trained parameters) and is much cheaper at inference than autoregressive decoding, replacing hundreds of sequential decode steps with one dense forward pass

Closure by construction: the graph readout's shared node instances make output rooms/walls closed by construction, turning a continuous coordinate problem into a checkable discrete edge-recall problem
Deterministic reconciliation eliminates double walls entirely (0 vs. 7.9/plan) and substantially raises watertightness and precision with no learned parameters
The edit-cost metric is argued to track real downstream human-correction effort better than raw F1
ResPlan-FP is redistributable (CC BY 4.0) unlike other floorplan raster corpora that are access-restricted
limitations: The two compared systems are not equally mature: the room-centric arm continues a published, more mature system, while the wall-first arm is the authors' own and its room/opening outputs are under-tuned

No experimental arm isolates training supervision alone, so earlier room-centric failures are attributed jointly to evaluation convention, reconciliation, and domain shift rather than to a single cause
Edit-cost operation weights are set by hand; ordering is shown robust across a weight sweep but calibration against real editor logs is left to future work
No arm was trained on clean ground-truth conditioning content alone, so training-time corruption cannot be fully ruled out as the reason input-side conditioning showed no benefit
ResPlan-FP splits are frozen by plan id without near-duplicate removal; ~6.9% near-duplicate plans are reported for the source corpus, which may inflate finetuned-track ceilings
Third-party baseline methods (HEAT, RoomFormer, Raster-to-Graph) have not yet been run on the new ResPlan-FP benchmark
The mechanism behind why the sequence decoder's learned style prior beats dense detection on clean, in-style renders is not further tested
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Several mechanisms are transferable by analogy even though the paper is 2D raster floorplan vectorization, not B-rep/CAD: (1) grammar/type-masked decoding that restricts the next token to what the output grammar allows at each step directly parallels our need for structural validity in the hexgen DSL decoder (e.g. masking to forbid referencing not-yet-emitted faces/points or duplicate IDs). (2) The training-free 'detect' readout -- reading structure from a dense/graph representation instead of full autoregressive emission -- is a useful design pattern for our pointer/copy addressing over the B-rep face graph, and their finding that autoregressive decoding degrades with output length while dense detection does not is a relevant caution for our program-length scaling. (3) Their deterministic post-hoc reconciliation/repair step (welding, dedup) that guarantees a validity property (no double walls) after generation is analogous to using our frozen verifier's checks as a deterministic repair pass rather than relying purely on generation-time validity. (4) Their closed-form condition for when combining two candidate outputs helps (donor purity > half the base F1) offers a reusable diagnostic for deciding when/how to fuse or select among best-of-N program candidates. (5) Their negative result on input-side conditioning (a deterministic re-encoding of the same evidence a model already sees adds no information, formalized via I(Y;D|X) <= H(D|X) = 0 for deterministic D) is a useful caution against expecting gains from feeding a decoder a second deterministic view of the same B-rep it already encodes, unless the added signal is genuinely new (e.g., stochastic search or execution feedback). (6) The edit-cost metric concept -- scoring drafts by repair effort rather than pass/fail -- could inspire an analogous 'verifier-fix-distance' metric for hexgen programs beyond binary structural validity.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is a single-author arXiv preprint (Aug 2026, not obviously peer reviewed) in an unrelated application domain (2D raster floorplan vectorization/CV), so nothing here is directly reusable as code or a component -- the value is purely as design-pattern inspiration. The two most transferable ideas are (a) grammar/type-masked autoregressive decoding for structural validity and (b) a training-free/lightweight 'detect' alternative to full autoregressive emission, both aligned with our top-priority structural-validity and pointer/graph-transformer problems. The negative input-side-conditioning result and the fusion purity condition are also worth keeping in mind when designing any candidate-combination or self-conditioning scheme for hexgen. Treat the applicability as analogical/tangential rather than a load-bearing citation.

provenance.method_summary: The network reuses the Raster2Seq backbone (ResNet features and a deformable-attention encoder)
provenance.key_architecture_choices: A type mask at every decoding step restricts the next token to what the grammar allows at that position, so the decoder cannot emit a duplicate wall ID
provenance.datasets: CubiCasa5K real scans, for which we release corrected skv4 annotations and the correction tooling
provenance.metrics: We report F1 over a tolerance sweep, watertightness read together with double-wall counts, and the edit-cost metric of Section 3.
provenance.headline_results: deterministic fusion of the two outputs raises wall F1 by 77 points over the better system alone (paired 95% interval
provenance.claimed_advantages: Because the readout replaces hundreds of sequential decoding steps with one dense forward pass, it is also much cheaper at inference than the decoder
provenance.limitations: the room-centric arm continues a published system from its released checkpoint, while the wall-first arm is ours and its room and opening outputs are under-tuned
provenance.implementation_cost_estimate: it has no trained parameter, produces walls with shared node instances, and takes rooms as the faces of the resulting planar graph
provenance.dependencies_on_other_methods: Raster2Seq [4], continued from its released checkpoint on the same data regimes, emits labeled room polygons and door and window polygons
provenance.code_link: Code, the benchmark, and the corrected annotations are available at https://github.com/Cyprinus12138/fpvec-lab.

payload.impact_rationale: A DAgger-style transition-system-masked policy plus a proof-aggregation self-improvement loop could meaningfully raise structural validity and cut rejection-sampling cost, but the gain is a template borrowed from a different domain (theorem proving), not a drop-in win.
payload.effort_rationale: Requires reframing the DSL decoder as a masked transition system and building a proof-aggregation/DAgger retraining loop around the frozen verifier -- a real but bounded engineering project.

payload.impact_rationale: Swapping/augmenting best-of-N sampling with grammar-constrained beam search at matched budget is shown to raise accuracy under a hard structural grammar, directly targeting our validity/compute tradeoff, though gains shrink with model capacity.
payload.effort_rationale: Beam search over an already grammar-masked decoder is a moderate, well-scoped implementation change to our existing decoding loop, not a new subsystem.

payload.impact_rationale: A training-free, LLM/critic-free scoring heuristic over already-sampled candidates (prefix alignment + fragment reuse + a floor that keeps every rule reachable) could improve best-of-N search efficiency and robustness to weak samples without extra model calls.
payload.effort_rationale: The method is symbolic/CFG-grammar search machinery; porting the scoring idea into our neural pointer/copy graph-decoding search loop needs real adaptation engineering, not a port.

payload.impact_rationale: Relative geometry-aware attention biases could help the encoder disambiguate congruent/symmetric faces when pointing, and a soft alignment-style regularizer could push generation toward our verifier's geometric criteria before best-of-N screening -- plausible but unproven on our task.
payload.effort_rationale: Both borrowed pieces (an MLP pairwise-offset attention bias, an auxiliary alignment loss) are small, self-contained additions to an existing graph-transformer encoder/decoder.

payload.impact_rationale: Verifier-replayed filtering of candidate branches before imitation, plus a post-imitation self-improvement DPO stage scored by the same frozen verifier, is the closest analog among this batch to hexgen's own verifier-in-the-loop design, and its ablation shows verifier-only scoring already captures most of the gain -- encouraging evidence for our current frozen-verifier-only bet.
payload.effort_rationale: Requires building a second training stage (self-sampling, verifier-scored DPO pairs) on top of the existing SFT pipeline and frozen verifier -- a moderate, well-precedented project.

payload.impact_rationale: Grammar/type-masked decoding and a deterministic post-hoc reconciliation/repair pass are concrete, low-risk validity levers directly analogous to our DSL masking and verifier-repair setup, though the paper's headline result (favoring a training-free 'detect' readout over autoregressive emission) argues against our core autoregressive/pointer-decoder architecture rather than for it.
payload.effort_rationale: The transferable pieces (decoder masking, a deterministic repair pass, a fusion/selection heuristic among candidates) are each small additions; the reviewer flags the readout comparison as inconclusive rather than a full method to build.
